items.explain: They collect regular blood pressure pills, and readings improve somewhat, as long as they keep a usable mailing address.
Their informal help at the library becomes an official volunteer role, and their days shrink to a fixed library routine.
The person is screened after contact with someone with a long cough, and may need follow-up treatment for a hidden infection.
The person stays homeless, with a low-priority housing application that does not move up the long waiting list.
A supportive librarian may leave, the person loses informal protection at the library, and goes back to sleeping under an underpass.
After missing blood pressure pills while without a stable address, the person suffers a warning stroke and is admitted to hospital.
The person dies of a stroke after years of high blood pressure and homelessness, likely near the shelter or library.
A child-protection referral is closed without a visit, easing the person's fear of losing custody, though complaints remain on file.
The person repays debts through small weekly deductions, clearing them by late 2055 if work hours hold up.
Once their immediate problems are fixed, the person drifts away from the tenants' group and stops pursuing complaints.
The person stays on antidepressants long-term, with persistent low mood and poor sleep from work and solo parenting.
The person keeps doing home care on unpredictable hours, never gets a secure contract, and relies on benefits to get by.
The person's son becomes an adult and leaves home, leaving them living alone in council housing, still doing care work.

items.plain: Leaves work due to ill health
items.explain: Years of physical strain, stress and low pay cause high blood pressure and injuries, forcing the person onto sickness benefits.
They start official agency work but, due to a background check note, may only work on one supervised crew.
Investigators decide some cash deposits were unreported earnings, leading to a small repayment plan or a formal warning.
After losing official income, they go back to old contacts and off-the-books cash work that authorities cannot track.
The person loses their rented room and ends up sleeping rough on and off.
The person joins a tenants' protest outside the council building with a neighbour.
The person keeps taking methadone daily at a set clinic time, with clean drug tests and dose reduction put on hold.
Police stop and search the person again, finding nothing, as protest involvement makes them more noticeable while on a suspended sentence.
The person meets their daughter and grandson again at Christmas, allowed only while drug tests stay clean.
Their library volunteering application is never answered, so they spend spare time on tenant organising instead.
The person's seasonal cash work ends, leaving no income and nothing structuring the day except the clinic visit.
Without work or routine, the person starts using opioids again, at high overdose risk from lowered tolerance, and loses family contact.
They rely on a chosen neighbour, not the official volunteer, to pick up their antidepressants occasionally.
A neighbour's daughter who helped collect medicine moves away to university, leaving them with one fewer local connection.
The person updates their will themselves, delayed but not stopped by a long wait for legal help.
Their only remaining helper neighbour faces job and marriage troubles, becoming less available, with nobody to replace that support.
The person falls or suddenly worsens at home and is hospitalised, weakened by weight loss, untreated blood pressure and poor mobility.
With no family nearby, the person goes from hospital into a care home and their house is put up for sale.
The person dies at 87 in 2056 from heart failure, worsened by being unable to look after themselves.
